//: CODE-002. Type checking for JavaScript, through JSDoc - not a TypeScript rewrite.
`checkJs` makes the compiler read the .js files that are already here and report what
it can prove wrong: a property that does not exist on the object, a call with the
wrong number of arguments, a value used as the wrong kind of thing. `noEmit` means it
never writes a file; it only answers questions.
`include` is deliberately short. Turning this on over two hundred files at once would
produce a wall of findings, and a wall gets silenced rather than read. It starts with
modules where a wrong shape costs the most - the ones that decide what is written to
disk and who may call what - and grows one module at a time, each addition being its
own small piece of work.
The provider adapters (wallhaven, gelbooru, danbooru, and provider-registry which
pulls them in) are NOT in scope yet, for a specific reason rather than convenience:
they `require` the bundled key files, which are gitignored. With JSON resolution on,
the compiler infers those files' shape from whatever happens to sit on this machine;
with it off, it cannot find them at all. Either way the answer would depend on an
untracked file, and a gate whose result depends on that is not a gate. Bringing them
in means giving those two requires a declared shape first - a small job of its own.
`strict` stays off for now on purpose. With it on, the first run would be thousands of
'this might be undefined' notes about code that has been working for a year, and the
real findings would be lost among them. What is on already catches the class this task
exists for. Tightening is the next step, per module, not a flag flipped in one go.
Adding `any` to silence a finding is not an acceptable way to pass this.
